video.title: Coiling | Spinal Motion | Eye Dominance | Arm Slot - 15 Serves Explained

classification.reason: The coach provides explicit actionable cues and drill recommendations, such as using a pure-dextral pinpoint stance, throwing the chest to the sky, and setting a 90/90 arm prep.

problem.title_as_question: How should you adapt your serve mechanics to your personal ocular dominance, spinal mobility, and arm slot?
problem.definition: Blindly copying professional serves—especially Federer's deep coiling—causes recreational servers to lose target vision and mechanical efficiency unless technique is matched to their eye dominance, spinal mobility, and shoulder plane.
problem.target_player: Players struggling with serve accuracy, velocity, or power leakage due to misaligned mechanics or copying incompatible pro styles

symptoms.description: Server loses peripheral vision of the opponent and service box, resulting in inaccurate targeting and awkward motion.
Arm elevates out of the shoulder line rather than rotating within the shoulder plane, sapping rotational velocity.
Upper spine stays flat or neutral during the cocking phase without thoracic extension, eliminating upward trunk spring.

causes.statement: Failing to spring-load the trunk with thoracic extension and backward side bending removes upward acceleration.
Moving the hitting arm out of plane relative to the shoulder line instead of titling the shoulders reduces rotational efficiency.
Treating forearm pronation or leg drive as the primary engine instead of the trunk and reactive shoulder rotation limits serve velocity.
Right-eye dominant players copying cross-dextral coil twist their upper torso away, cutting off peripheral vision of the court.

angles.summary: Serve velocity is primarily powered by the trunk stretch-contracting and reactively whipping the shoulder from external to internal rotation, not by forearm pronation.
Copying Roger Federer's deep coiling is counterproductive for pure-dextral players because turning the upper body away completely blinds their dominant right eye.
High contact should be achieved via a cartwheel shoulder tilt rather than raising the arm independently above the shoulder line.
Jakub Mensik demonstrates the pure-dextral pinpoint stance by stepping his rear foot to the hitting side to coil without blinding his rear eye.
Thinking of the serve as throwing the chest to the sky promotes upward thoracic extension rather than dumping rotation forward.

solutions.summary: If right-eye dominant, keep your head, chest, and eyes oriented more forward toward the court during prep to maintain peripheral vision.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the service box and opponent in peripheral view with the back eye

solutions.summary: Practice the pure-dextral pinpoint footwork by stepping your back foot onto the hitting side of your front foot to coil without turning away from the net.
solutions.external_goal: Step back foot across to the hitting side into an open-stance base

solutions.summary: Cue yourself to throw your chest to the sky into the cocking phase to engage thoracic extension and drive upward acceleration.
solutions.external_goal: Point the chest up toward the sky during the windup

solutions.summary: Simplify early prep by placing the hitting arm directly into a 90/90 position before throwing to guarantee arm-shoulder plane alignment.
solutions.external_goal: Set 90 degrees at the elbow and upper arm during prep
